Study identifies ocean temperature gradient as a driver of tropical Atlantic climate

A study highlighted by NOAA finds that the north-to-south sea-surface temperature gradient is an important driver of tropical Atlantic climate, including hurricane activity and Sahel rainfall.

A clearer link between ocean patterns, storms and rainfall could improve understanding of risks that cross regions and affect communities, agriculture and planning.

Could tracking this temperature gradient help connect Atlantic conditions to rainfall risks in the Sahel?

Study maps heat-related deaths by workers’ occupation

A study published in JAMA used U.S. surveillance data to examine heat-related mortality among working-age people, broken down by occupation and industry, for 2021–2023.

Occupation-specific evidence can reveal where workplace protections and heat planning may need to be targeted as high temperatures affect labor, health and productivity.

Could better identification of at-risk jobs change how employers plan work during extreme heat?

Nobel Prize recognizes research that made brain activity controllable with light

The 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine recognized work on optogenetics, a research approach that uses light to control and study activity in specific cells.

The method has helped researchers investigate neural circuits with precision, supporting new lines of basic neuroscience and potential future research into brain disorders.

What new questions become testable when researchers can switch specific neural activity on and off?

AI infrastructure investment is extending beyond chips and power into construction supply chains and labor demand, spreading its economic effects across sectors.

items.linkedin_text:
NOAA releases updated global ocean-carbon data products

NOAA and international collaborators published updated versions of the Surface Ocean CO₂ Atlas and a global ocean carbon data product. The agency says the datasets will improve monitoring of ocean carbon cycles and understanding of ocean change.

Better observations can sharpen climate and ocean forecasts, informing research and decisions that depend on tracking how much carbon the ocean absorbs.

How might improved carbon measurements change projections of the ocean’s role in climate regulation?
